transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2027-08-21 15:30 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Maya, Jorge, Priya (Redwood); Liam, Rashida, Evan, Sara, Tom (CardinalMed)

Summary: quick audit of network + runtime latency sources. We ran through a model of their private VPC topology and hypothesized where the 120-180ms spikes are coming from.

[00:00] Maya: alright everyone, thanks for making time, this is the subnet/private link latency audit. real quick we'll run through the topology you sent, then look at KV cache behavior, and then go into batching + quantization impacts.
[00:14] Liam: yep, thanks, uh we saw a lot of p99 jumps on our edge tests, roughly 200 ms spikes intermittently, sometimes worse during bulk ingest.
[00:27] Jorge: yeah and just to call out, sometimes those numbers are from DNS retry or hairpinning across the NAT, so good to confirm exact packet path.
[00:38] Rashida: one thing: our VPC has three subnets per AZ, we do PrivateLink for the control plane, and egress goes through a central NAT in a shared services account.
[00:51] Priya: ok, so shared NAT, Private Link, and split subnets — classic. two quick questions: do you have source/dest checks disabled on the NAT instances, and are you using AWS-managed NAT gateway or self-hosted?
[01:05] Tom: managed NAT gateway for now, but we do have a small fleet of NAT instances in one AZ for failover, it's been fine but we skipped MTU tuning.
[01:18] Jorge: MTU tuning can bite you with large protobuf payloads — seen cases where fragmentation and reassembly add tens of ms. also note, Private Link adds an additional hop into the service VPC which can add 8-20ms depending on AZ pairing.
[01:33] Evan: question about KV cache: our experience is that cold misses spike latency a lot because the runtime backfills from object storage; how much of that is network vs runtime CPU?
[01:45] Priya: good call — it's both. if you have cold KV misses that trigger a disk or S3 fetch, network to S3 and the object size matters. but also the runtime's cache miss path includes serialization and de-dup work. we usually instrument both sides.
[01:59] Sara: and on security, we use customer-managed KMS, want to make sure encryption ops aren't the bottleneck.
[02:06] Jorge: KMS calls are out-of-band and usually a handful of ms, unless you do synchronous decrypts at high QPS. recommend doing envelope encryption where the runtime caches data keys.
[02:20] Liam: can you explain the hairpinning we suspected? I think our packets go out to NAT and then back into the same AZ to hit the PrivateLink?
[02:28] Maya: yes — typical pattern: client in private subnet -> NAT -> PrivateLink endpoint in shared services AZ -> service ENI -> back to target subnet. That extra egress/ingress can cause cross-AZ latency and double NAT.
[02:43] Tom: so is double NAT the real offender? we can't move to dedicated links easily.
[02:48] Jorge: not always. double NAT can add ~10-30 ms; combined with MTU issues and DNS timeouts you're compounding. The p99 spikes you saw could be a confluence.
[03:02] Priya: we should also look at DNS. If you depend on the default VPC resolver with recursion plus PrivateLink, some lookups get forwarded externally causing 50-100ms tail calls. configure AmazonProvidedDNS with conditional forwarding to avoid external hops.
[03:17] Rashida: we do have conditional forwarding set up but we recently changed the resolver to use an internal resolver in the shared services account — might be a misroute.
[03:27] Jorge: that would explain intermittent long tails. also check the TTLs on the endpoints — low TTLs increase queries.
[03:38] Evan: switching to runtime / kvcache — we observed cold miss added 80-120ms per request on average; warm hits are sub-5ms. is that normal?
[03:47] Priya: yes that's in the expected ballpark if cold path pulls from S3. If you use local SSD-backed caching in the runtime, cold miss is more like 20-40ms instead. Our recommendation: pre-warm top-k keys for your throughput profile.
[04:00] Liam: we have batching at the inference client set to batch size 8 with a 40ms wait. does that interact with KV cache behavior?
[04:09] Jorge: batching helps amortize KV lookups across multiple inferences if you can coalesce keys, but it also increases tail for individual requests. with batch size 8 and a 40ms Batching window your p50 might look great but p99 can shoot up, especially if one request in the batch triggers an S3 backfill.
[04:25] Tom: so we should maybe disable batching for low-latency endpoints and enable it for throughput endpoints?
[04:31] Priya: exactly — create distinct routes: L-AT (low-latency, no batch, higher cost) and HT (throughput, batch, quantize). Redwood supports per-route policies so you can pin models and batching configs.
[04:45] Sara: any thoughts on quantization for our clinical model? we're worried about quality regressions but need cost/time improvements.
[04:53] Maya: safe approach: 8-bit quantization + eval set focused on clinical prompts. quantized model typically reduces token latency per step by around 20-30% on GPU inference and can increase throughput 2-3x depending on kernel support. but you should run end-to-end evals on the same prompt sets.
[05:12] Evan: what's the impact on jitter? our users are sensitive to bursty latency.
[05:18] Jorge: quantization can reduce jitter because compute time per token becomes more predictable, but if you combine it with aggressive batching, you'll still see variable tails due to queueing.
[05:29] Rashida: about on-prem: we have a single rack with 2x A100s and a 10Gb uplink to our edge. will that be enough for low-latency inference?
[05:37] Priya: single rack can be fine for moderate traffic, but network oversubscription on the 10Gb uplink might be the limiting factor. for KV cache traffic and model weights pulls you want a separate management plane network or QoS rules to prioritize inference traffic.
[05:55] Tom: ok, do you have a recommended subnet layout? we have three AZs in prod but want minimal cross-AZ for inference paths.
[06:04] Jorge: recommend colocating inference pools and PrivateLink endpoints in the same AZs. Use per-AZ dedicated subnets with local route tables and local NAT gateways if possible — avoids cross-AZ egress and reduces hops. If you must centralize NAT, use high-availability NAT instances with source/dest checks disabled and ensure MTU is tuned to 9001 if you use jumbo frames.
[06:26] Liam: do you have a fallback policy suggestion if a PrivateLink endpoint goes unhealthy? we saw timeouts cascade.
[06:33] Maya: yes, Redwood supports policy-based fallbacks: route to a regional hosted model (higher cost) or to a warmed secondary PrivateLink endpoint. Configure short circuiting: after N failed connections in M seconds, fall back immediately rather than waiting for TCP timeouts.
[06:47] Sara: from a compliance angle, we need audit logs for all model requests and key access. can Redwood's Private deployment keep request-level logs without sending payloads to control plane?
[06:56] Priya: yes, in Private mode logs stay in your account and you can enable payload-less auditing. we also support SAML SSO and role-based RBAC integrated with your IdP.
[07:07] Evan: let's talk microbench steps — what do you want us to run?
[07:11] Jorge: three tests: 1) synthetic p95 latency with 1QPS steady-state, 2) 3-hour spike test with 200 concurrent clients to reproduce p99 tails, and 3) cold-start KV miss sweep where you clear cache and run a burst to observe backfill latency. Collect tcpdump, pcap, traceroute, and runtime traces (flamegraphs).
[07:30] Rashida: ok we'll do those. question on traces: where do you want them uploaded?
[07:34] Maya: upload to the shared CardinalMed-Redwood drive, I'll send link. include timestamps for alignment with our logs.
[07:40] Tom: side note: our EKS nodes have Calico and some egress policies; are there common misconfigs you see there?
[07:46] Jorge: yes, default egress rules sometimes force SNAT for intra-cluster traffic; ensure your pod CIDR isn't SNATed when talking to service IPs in the same VPC. also watch for DNS policy set to default vs ClusterFirstWithHostNet — they change where queries go.
[08:00] Liam: for the benchmarking, any particular metrics to surface? we care about p50/p95/p99, jitter, and error rate, plus token cost.
[08:08] Priya: include p50/p90/p95/p99, tail loss rate, CPU/GPU utilization, KV cache hit ratio over time, queue depth, and network retransmits. Also export the runtime batch size distribution.
[08:22] Sara: for the KV cache instrumentation, can you give an example span naming scheme?
[08:27] Jorge: use something like runtime.kv.lookup.{hit|miss|backfill} with tags for keyshard and latency_ms, capture stack trace for misses over 100ms. we'll share an instrumentation snippet.
[08:40] Evan: one more — are there any edge cases where PrivateLink TLS handshake causes big latency bumps?
[08:46] Priya: if you do full mTLS with OCSP checks for each handshake, that will add tens of ms. recommended: mutual TLS with session resumption and long-lived connections. also SNI mismatches can cause route flapping.
[08:58] Tom: good to know.
[09:00] Maya: ok wrapping up, recap: we'll send the CFN template, KV snippet, and a suggested per-AZ subnet layout. Customer will run three bench tests and upload artifacts. follow-up next week to review results.
[09:14] Liam: thanks everyone.
[09:16] Rashida: small ask — include the example route table entries you recommend in the doc.
[09:20] Maya: will do. thanks all.

End transcript. Notes: some timestamps are approximate. Minor transcription noise present (names sometimes 'Jorge A' or 'Priya S').
